title: Understanding and Controlling a Maze-Solving Policy Network
models: Procgen maze-solving policy from Langosco et al. (3.5M parameters, 15 conv layers, IMPALA blocks) that exhibits goal misgeneralization
methods: behavioral regression of goal choice at decision squares on maze features
activation-addition steering vectors (cheese vector, top-right vector)
question: What goals does a misgeneralizing maze policy pursue, where are they represented internally, and can those representations be edited to control behavior?
key_findings: Goal choice at decision squares is predictable from maze features: l1 logistic regression on three distances reaches 82.4% vs 71.4% for always predicting 'reaches cheese' (5K mazes, 10 splits); Euclidean distance to cheese matters beyond path distance.
11 of 128 channels after the first residual block of the second IMPALA block track the cheese location (redundant, distributed goal representation).

Resampling these channels from mazes with the cheese elsewhere changes the most likely action at decision squares in 40% of 200 mazes vs 11% when resampling from mazes with the cheese in the same place.
Setting one activation (of 32,768) in channel 55 to +5.5 partially retargets the policy toward the edited location.

Subtracting a 'cheese vector' (activation difference with vs without cheese) substantially lowers cheese-seeking action probability over 100 mazes, but adding it has no effect; adding a 'top-right vector' increases corner-seeking, subtracting it does not reduce it; the two edits combine without interference.

evidence.scale: 5K mazes for behavioral regression; 200 mazes for resampling; 100 mazes for steering vectors
evidence.statistics: partial: train/validation splits for regression; steering results shown as distributions, no formal tests
evidence.baselines: always-cheese predictor; resampling from same-location mazes; unmodified policy

causal_validation: Yes: activation resampling, single-activation edits and steering vectors change action probabilities and trajectories in predicted directions, with asymmetric effects reported honestly.
closed_loop: Partly: trajectory visualizations under edits; quantitative results are action probabilities at decision squares.
limitations_stated: Control is only partial; the retargeted network sometimes ignores the edited location.
Cheese-tracking channels also weakly affect behavior through factors other than cheese location.
critique: Classic early example of goal representations and activation steering in a policy network; the asymmetric steering results (subtracting works, adding does not) are an important caution for VLA steering papers that report only one direction.
Channel identification is by visual inspection; no systematic search or ablation of all channels.
Spatially aligned conv feature maps make goal location trivially readable; continuous-control VLAs lack this, as with the Sokoban and chess examples (2504.01871, 2406.00877).
one_line: A maze RL policy that sometimes goes to its old training goal instead of the cheese has 11 channels that track the cheese, and editing or resampling them, or subtracting a 'cheese vector', partly redirects where it goes.
